newsitem.title: USA: Gore travels to improve U.S. ties with China.
newsitem.headline: Gore travels to improve U.S. ties with China.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore on Saturday began an eight-day trip to Asia aimed at easing strains in U.S.-Sino relations, a task complicated by claims China illegally tried to influence the 1996 U.S. elections.
Gore departed from Andrews Air Force Base for Japan, where he was to discuss China policies and other issues with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday before heading to Beijing that night.
Gore's talks on Tuesday with Chinese President Jiang Zemin are the first prolonged U.S. discussions with Beijing's leader since the death of Deng Xiaoping, who died last month.
U.S. officials have been closly monitoring the situation in China for any hint that Jiang's power may be threatened now that Deng has passed away.
Gore quietly will be taking the measure of Jiang himself and his ability to fend off any would-be rivals, officials say.

"The most fundamental issue, of course, in post-Deng China is whether political reform will come, how soon," said Winston Lord, former assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific Affairs for the Clinton administration.
"Despite the fact that China has opened up, that political system remains opaque," said Lord. "We are due for surprises, we have been in the past."

A broad range of divisive issues, from trade to human rights, faces the mission led by Gore -- the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Beijing since army troops brutally ended pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
"Nothing is excluded" from Gore's agenda in China, a senior administration official said.
"These things will be dealt with the right way in terms of making sure that American concerns are clearly expressed," said the official, who accompanied Gore on the trip.

Gore aides said the vice president intended to raise the subject of China's alleged attempts to influence elections last year through campaign contributions -- including some into the campaign coffers of Gore and President Bill Clinton.
"It won't be confrontational," one official said. "He's on a diplomatic mission, but he'll certainly discuss the subject."

Congress and the FBI currently are looking into the charges, which the government of China has vigorously denied. The Democratic Party, however, was forced to return some $3 million in donations it said came from suspicious sources, several with Asian ties.
A primary purpose of the trip was to lay the groundwork for a state visit to Washington by Jiang later this year and a trip to Bejing by Clinton in 1998.

Concerns about the fundraising scandal involving China have dampened some of the expectations for the trip. Although U.S. officials had been negotiating with their Chinese counterparts trying to hammer out various agreements in time for Gore's trip, no dramatic breakthroughs are expected.

Gore's advisers had an internal debate over whether he should even participate in a signing ceremony in which China plans to order new planes from Boeing -- a move that will generate jobs and benefit the U.S. economy.
Although officials now say there is no question Gore would participate in such an event if a final contract is reached, the fact there was any doubt underscores the sensitivity of the trip.

"My guess is, not much will be achieved here, and that's okay," said Greg Mastel, an expert on China for the Economic Strategy Institute, about the visit. "It's important to have an important dialogue with the Chinese."
"The problems we have with the Chinese are not the kind of problems you can solve with a simple summit ... but just keeping the dialogue open is useful," he said.
